ncf62686cafa.s: In constitutionalism, a decision backed by a legislative majority:
ncf62686cafa.x: A majoritarian position cannot override constitutionalism; constitutional limits bind even a majority decision.

nindian-polity-75-11.x: Constitutional government is limited government: the constitution defines, restrains and checks power to prevent executive tyranny.

nindian-polity-75-33.s: The Rule of Law existed in India before PIL through which Articles?
nindian-polity-75-33.x: The rule of law existed before PIL through Articles 14, 32 and 226; PIL widens access to justice but is not indispensable for it.

n58d40919d69.s: The Governor's assent to Bills passed by the State Legislature is dealt with in Article:
n58d40919d69.x: Article 200 covers the Governor's assent; Article 111 is presidential assent and Article 201 covers Bills reserved for the President.

ne548d1308b7.s: Discussion in Parliament on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge, except on a removal motion, is barred by:
ne548d1308b7.x: Article 121 bars it in Parliament (Article 211 in State Legislatures); Article 122 stops courts questioning parliamentary procedure.

n751ca37f2ca.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Indian Constitution does not recognise a rigid separation of powers?
o: Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
n751ca37f2ca.x: Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) held there is no rigid separation of powers and executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.

nc3395760c43.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Advisory opinion to the President – Article 137
Advice under Article 143 – Binding on the President
Supreme Court review of its own judgment – Article 137
Supreme Court review of its own judgment – Article 143
nc3395760c43.x: The Supreme Court reviews its own judgments under Article 137; the President seeks its advice under Article 143, and that advice is not binding.

nindian-polity-8-5.s: The election of the President of India is:
o: A direct election by adult suffrage
An election by the Lok Sabha alone
nindian-polity-8-5.x: The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college; nominated MPs do not vote, and disputes go to the Supreme Court.

nindian-polity-36-8.s: Which of the following vote in the Presidential election?
nindian-polity-36-8.x: Elected MLAs vote; nominated MPs, nominated MLAs and all members of Legislative Councils do not.

n3697af0c1ac.s: The impeachment charge against the President must be passed in each House by:
o: An absolute majority of members present
Three-fourths of members present and voting
n3697af0c1ac.x: Under Article 61 each House must pass the charge by two-thirds of its total membership; a simple majority is not enough.

na6f65b81d98.s: A President elected to fill a vacancy caused by death or resignation holds office for:
o: A full term of five years
Until the next Lok Sabha election
na6f65b81d98.x: A President elected to fill a vacancy gets a full five-year term, not the unexpired part of the predecessor's term.

n3c0faaa496b.s: Who can grant a pardon in a court-martial case?
o: Both the President and the Governor
Neither the President nor the Governor
n3c0faaa496b.x: Only the President can pardon a court-martial sentence; the Governor has no such power.

nindian-polity-8-31.s: Which of the following does the President do on ministerial advice rather than as situational discretion?
o: Appointing a PM in a hung Parliament
Dismissing a government that has lost its majority
Dissolving the Lok Sabha in special situations
nindian-polity-8-31.x: Ambassadors are appointed on ministerial advice; the other three are situations of limited discretion.

n976b086a951.s: The two-term limit on the President of the United States comes from its:
n976b086a951.x: The Twenty-Second Amendment limits a US President to two terms; South Korea has a single five-year term.

n3c733b3207a.s: In constitutional terminology, the term 'impeachment' is used for the removal of:
n3c733b3207a.x: Impeachment is used only for the President; judges and the Vice-President are 'removed'.

nindian-polity-2-39.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 66 – There shall be a Vice-President
Article 67 – Vice-President to act as President
Article 65 – Vice-President to act as President
nindian-polity-2-39.x: Article 65 covers the Vice-President acting as President; Article 63 creates the office, 66 covers the election and 67 the term and removal.

nindian-polity-8-23.s: The President's appointment of the majority party leader as Prime Minister rests on:
nindian-polity-8-23.x: Appointing the majority leader as PM is a convention; Article 78 is the separate right to seek information from the PM.

nindian-polity-8-30.s: The President declares war and concludes peace on the advice of the:
nindian-polity-8-30.x: Sequence was not possible as the facts carry no dates. The President, as Supreme Commander, declares war and makes peace on the Council of Ministers' advice.

o: A temporary stay of execution of a sentence
Removal of both sentence and conviction
Substitution of a lighter form of punishment
Reduction of the period without changing its character
nindian-polity-38-16.x: A reprieve only postpones execution temporarily; removal of sentence and conviction is a pardon.

nindian-polity-38-39.s: Which form of pardoning power removes both the sentence and the conviction?
nindian-polity-38-39.x: A pardon removes both sentence and conviction; a reprieve only postpones execution.

ne1c0cf7895c.s: What time limit does the Constitution fix for the President to decide on an Ordinary Bill?
ne1c0cf7895c.x: Article 111 prescribes no time limit, which is why the pocket veto works in India.

n7f1316ec5e9.s: The real or de facto executive in India is the:
o: Prime Minister heading the Council of Ministers
n7f1316ec5e9.x: The President is the nominal (de jure) executive; the PM with the Council of Ministers is the real (de facto) executive.

n631c73a2aaa.s: Under Article 74(2), the advice tendered by Ministers to the President:
o: Cannot be inquired into by any court
Can be inquired into by the Supreme Court only
Can be inquired into by a High Court
n631c73a2aaa.x: Article 74(2) says whether and what advice was tendered cannot be inquired into by any court.

nindian-polity-8-7.s: The Vice-President acts as President when the office falls vacant under Article:
nindian-polity-8-7.x: Article 65 lets the Vice-President act as President; Article 63 creates the office, 64 makes him RS Chairman, 66 covers his election.

ndf6b7cff9fb.s: Over a Money Bill passed by Parliament, the President can:
o: Assent or withhold assent, but not return it
Keep it pending only for ten days
ndf6b7cff9fb.x: For a Money Bill the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration.

n55d7a182653.s: Which Amendment made the President's assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory?
n55d7a182653.x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made assent mandatory; the President cannot reject or return such a Bill.

n2200692685e.s: In 2025 the Supreme Court held that a Governor's indefinite inaction on a Bill is justiciable under Article:
n2200692685e.x: Indefinite inaction under Article 200 is justiciable, so the Governor has no presidential-style pocket veto.

nindian-polity-74-10.s: Which of the following can an ordinance NOT do?
nindian-polity-74-10.x: Within legislative competence an ordinance can amend Acts, act retrospectively and change taxes, but it cannot amend the Constitution.

n05bbf7e184e.s: The veto of the President of the United States can be overridden by:
n05bbf7e184e.x: The US President has a qualified veto, which Congress can override by a two-thirds majority.

nindian-polity-64-18.s: Under Article 101(4), an MP's seat may be vacated after unexcused absence of:
nindian-polity-64-18.x: Unexcused absence for 60 days can vacate the seat; prorogation and adjournments of more than four consecutive days are left out of the count.

new.s: Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of Laws' was published in:
new.x: Montesquieu set out the division of powers in 'The Spirit of Laws' (1748), drawing on the British constitution.

new.s: Article 50, which directs separation of the judiciary from the executive, is a:
o: Provision of the Union Executive chapter
new.x: Article 50 is a DPSP directing the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.

new.s: In which year did the Madras Presidency separate the Collector's judicial powers?
new.x: The Madras Presidency separated the Collector's judicial powers in 1816, an early separation in the Andhra districts.

new.s: Ambedkar preferred the parliamentary system because it gives priority to:
new.x: Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability, helped by familiarity with the 1919 and 1935 Acts.

new.s: In India, the executive is subordinate to the:
new.x: In the parliamentary system the executive is drawn from and accountable to the legislature, so it is subordinate to it.

new.s: Collective responsibility of a State Council of Ministers to the Legislative Assembly is provided under Article:
new.x: Article 164(2) is the State counterpart of Article 75(3), which covers the Union Council of Ministers.

new.s: Which legislative device removes the President of India?
new.x: Impeachment under Article 61 removes the President; a no-confidence motion removes the government.

new.s: Under Article 85, the maximum gap between two sessions of Parliament is:
new.x: Article 85 (Article 174 for States) allows at most a six-month gap between sessions.

new.s: The President's address and messages to Parliament are provided under Articles:
new.x: Articles 86 and 87 cover the President's address and messages; Articles 175 and 176 are the State equivalents.

new.s: Which of the following pairs (Union – State) is INCORRECTLY matched?
new.x: Collective responsibility is Art. 75(3) for the Union and Art. 164(2) for States, not 163(2).

new.s: The power of the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha is contained in Article:
new.x: Article 85(2) provides for dissolution of the lower House; Article 85(1) deals with summoning.

new.s: Courts cannot question the proceedings of Parliament on the ground of irregular procedure under Article:
new.x: Article 122 (212 for States) shields legislative procedure from courts; Articles 121 and 211 bar legislatures from discussing judges.

new.s: Judicial review of laws and executive action in India rests mainly on Articles:
new.x: Judicial review rests on Articles 13, 32 and 226, and a law found ultra vires is void.

new.s: In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court struck down the validation of the PM's election made by the:
new.x: Raj Narain held the legislature cannot decide an election dispute and struck down the 39th Amendment's validation.

new.s: Separation of powers was held to be a basic feature of the Constitution in:
new.x: Kesavananda (1973) treated separation of powers as a basic feature; Ram Jawaya Kapur only held there is no rigid separation.

new.s: Under I.R. Coelho, Ninth Schedule entries made after which date are open to judicial review?
new.x: I.R. Coelho made laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 reviewable.

new.s: Which Constitutional Amendment overrode the Golaknath judgment?
new.x: The 24th overrode Golaknath; the 1st overrode Champakam Dorairajan, the 26th Madhav Rao and the 77th Indra Sawhney.

new.s: The 26th Amendment, abolishing privy purses, overrode the judgment in:
new.x: The 26th Amendment overrode Madhav Rao (privy purses).

new.s:
Consider the following statements about overriding a judgment:
1. A validating law must remove the basis of the judgment.
2. A validating law may simply declare a judgment void.
3. Advice given under Article 143 is not binding on the President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
new.x: 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: a validating law cannot simply declare a judgment void.

new.s: The electoral college for the 16th Vice-Presidential election (2022) had how many members?
new.x: The 16th VP election (2022) had an electoral college of 788 members, all MPs.

new.s: The Vice-President addresses his resignation to the:
new.x: The Vice-President resigns to the President; the President resigns to the Vice-President.

new.s: The Vice-President is removed by:
o: A Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha
An order of the Supreme Court
new.x: The VP is removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha; impeachment applies only to the President.

new.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Vice-President?
o: Nominated MPs vote in his election
Elected MLAs vote in his election
He is not a part of Parliament
There is no six-month deadline to fill his vacancy
new.x: No MLAs vote for the Vice-President; his electoral college is all MPs, elected and nominated.

new.s: A candidate for Vice-President needs how many proposers and seconders?
new.x: A VP candidate needs 20 + 20; a Presidential candidate needs 50 + 50.

new.s: An ordinance promulgated by the President lapses how long after Parliament reassembles?
new.x: An ordinance must be laid before Parliament and lapses six weeks after reassembly unless approved.

new.s: Repeated re-promulgation of ordinances in Bihar was held a fraud on the Constitution in:
new.x: D.C. Wadhwa (1987) held routine re-promulgation in Bihar a fraud on the Constitution.

new.s: Krishna Kumar Singh (2017), holding that laying an ordinance is mandatory, was decided by a bench of:
new.x: Seven judges decided Krishna Kumar Singh (5:2): laying is mandatory and the satisfaction is reviewable.

new.s:
Consider the following statements about the ordinance-making power:
1. The President may withdraw an ordinance at any time.
2. An ordinance is not subject to judicial review.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
new.x: Only 1 is correct: an ordinance may be withdrawn any time, and it is subject to judicial review.

new.s: The oath of office of the President is administered by the:
new.x: Under Article 60 the CJI (or the senior-most SC judge) administers the oath, not the Vice-President.

new.s: The emoluments of the President are listed in which Schedule of the Constitution?
new.x: Emoluments are fixed by Parliament by law, listed in the Second Schedule and charged on the Consolidated Fund.

new.s: The President's salary, fixed by the Finance Act, 2018, is:
new.x: The Finance Act, 2018 fixed the President's salary at ₹5 lakh per month from 1 January 2016.

new.s: Which Article bars the President from being a member of any legislature and provides a rent-free residence?
new.x: Article 59 sets the conditions of office; Article 58 is qualifications, 57 re-election and 60 the oath.

new.s: When a President's term expires, who holds the office until the successor enters it?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
new.x: Under Article 56 the outgoing President continues until his successor enters office.

new.s: After President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office, who acted as President?
new.x: Vice-President B.D. Jatti acted as President after Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office.

new.s: The executive power of the Union is vested in the President by Article:
new.x: Article 53 vests the executive power; Article 52 creates the office and 54 sets the electoral college.

new.s: Which Article makes it the Prime Minister's duty to keep the President informed?
new.x: Article 78 is the PM's duty to inform; 77 is conduct of business, 76 the Attorney-General.

new.s: The 15% size limit on the Council of Ministers in Article 75(1A) was added by the:
new.x: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A) capping the Council of Ministers at 15%.

new.s: Election Commissioners are appointed by the President under Article:
new.x: Article 324 covers Election Commissioners; 148 is the CAG, 76 the AG and 155 Governors.

new.s: Under the Third Judges Case (1998), the collegium consulted for appointing Supreme Court judges consists of:
o: The CJI and four senior-most judges
The CJI and two senior-most judges
The CJI and the Law Minister
new.x: The Third Judges Case (1998) set the collegium as the CJI plus four senior-most judges.

new.s:
Consider the following statements about Presidential election disputes:
1. Election disputes of the President are decided only by the Supreme Court.
2. Acts done by a President before his election is declared void become invalid.
3. The election cannot be challenged because of vacancies in the electoral college.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
new.x: 1 and 3 are correct (Arts. 71 and 71(4)). Statement 2 is wrong: acts done before the election is declared void remain valid.

new.s: Elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry were added to the President's electoral college by the:
new.x: The 70th Amendment (1992) added the elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry.

new.s: Before 1997, a Presidential candidate's nomination needed:
new.x: It was 10 + 10 before 1997; since then it is 50 proposers and 50 seconders.

new.s: Who was the first President of India from South India?
new.x: S. Radhakrishnan (1962–67), earlier the first Vice-President, was the first President from South India.

new.s: Who was the first President of India to die in office?
new.x: Zakir Husain (1967–69) was the first to die in office; Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed also later died in office.

new.s: N. Sanjiva Reddy, the only President elected unopposed, came from which district of Andhra Pradesh?
new.x: N. Sanjiva Reddy, from Anantapur, was elected in 1977 and was the first CM of Andhra Pradesh (1956).

new.s: Which President won the election on second-preference votes?
new.x: V.V. Giri (1969) won on second-preference votes under the single transferable vote.

new.s: Which veto does the President of India NOT possess?
new.x: The qualified veto (overridable by a higher majority) is a US feature; the Indian President has the other three.

new.s: In Kehar Singh (1989), the Supreme Court held that a mercy petitioner before the President:
o: Has no right of oral hearing
Has a right of oral hearing
Must be heard by the Supreme Court first
new.x: Kehar Singh held the President may examine evidence afresh but there is no right of oral hearing.

new.s: The suspensive veto of the President applies to:
new.x: The suspensive veto (return once) applies only to Ordinary Bills, not Money Bills.

new.s: The rule that a Bill becomes law if not decided within 10 days is a feature of:
new.x: The 10-day rule is a US feature; Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the Indian President.

new.s: The absolute veto of the President is usually applied to:
new.x: The absolute veto is used for private members' Bills and for Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent.

new.s: The President's one-time power to return a Bill can apply to Financial Bills of:
new.x: The one-time return power can apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II; Money Bills cannot be returned.

new.s: Dr. Rajendra Prasad exercised the absolute veto on the:
new.x: Rajendra Prasad used the absolute veto on the PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954, on the Council of Ministers' advice.

new.s: For a State Bill reserved by the Governor, the President declares or withholds assent under Article:
new.x: Article 201 governs reserved State Bills; Article 200 is the Governor's own options.

new.s: In the November 2025 Presidential reference under Article 143, the Supreme Court held that courts:
o: Can fix a three-month timeline for assent
Can declare pending Bills deemed assented
Can direct the President to assent to any Bill
Cannot fix timelines for the Governor or the President
new.x: The five-judge bench held courts cannot fix timelines and there is no deemed assent, though the powers cannot be used arbitrarily.

new.s: In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor (8 April 2025), how many Tamil Nadu Bills were deemed assented?
new.x: The April 2025 ruling held indefinite inaction under Article 200 justiciable and deemed ten TN Bills assented.

new.s: The pardoning power of the President under Article 72 is:
o: An executive power exercised in his discretion
A judicial power exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice
A legislative power of the Executive
A power exercised on the Supreme Court's advice
new.x: Article 72 is a judicial power of the President, exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice.

new.s: Reducing a sentence of two years' rigorous imprisonment to one year's rigorous imprisonment is:
new.x: Remission shortens the period without changing the character; commutation changes the form.

new.s: Which form of pardoning power substitutes a lighter form of punishment?
new.x: Commutation changes the form (death to rigorous life imprisonment); remission only reduces the period.

new.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Pardon – Removes both sentence and conviction
new.x: Respite is a lesser sentence for special reasons like pregnancy or disability; a temporary stay of execution is a reprieve.

new.s:
Consider the following statements about the pardoning power under Article 72:
1. Article 72 covers sentences by court-martial.
2. Amnesty falls within Article 72.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
new.x: Only 1 is correct: Article 72 covers court-martial, Union-law offences and death sentences; amnesty is outside it.

new.s: The Governor's pardoning power is provided under Article:
new.x: Article 161 gives the Governor pardoning power for offences against State laws.

new.s: In respect of a death sentence, the Governor can NOT:
new.x: The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence but can suspend, remit or commute it; only the President can pardon it.

new.s: Limited judicial review of pardons on mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds was laid down in:
o: Epuru Sudhakar v Govt of AP (2006)
new.x: Epuru Sudhakar (2006), an AP case, allows limited judicial review of pardons.

new.s: In Maru Ram (1980), the Supreme Court held that the pardoning power is exercised:
o: On the Council of Ministers' advice
On the advice of the Supreme Court
On the advice of the Home Secretary
new.x: Maru Ram held the power is exercised on the Council of Ministers' advice.

new.s: Which veto does the Indian President have but the US President does not?
new.x: India has an absolute veto, which the USA lacks; the USA has a qualified veto, which India lacks.

new.s: The President can withdraw an ordinance:
o: Only within six weeks of reassembly
new.x: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time; saying he cannot is a common trap.

new.s: The maximum life of an ordinance is:
new.x: Six months (maximum gap between sessions) plus six weeks after reassembly gives the maximum life.
